title: Four cubits (Berakhot 8a)
hook: since the Temple fell, God has only the four cubits of halakha in the world
tomorrow: a sword at your neck. is it too late to ask?

segments.voice: Yesterday: even God wants a blessing. Ishmael blessed God in the Temple's innermost room. But what happens when there's no Temple at all?
screen: `BLESS THE ONE ABOVE.` → `AND WHEN THE TEMPLE IS GONE?`

segments.voice: A new apartment, half the size of the old house. Boxes on every surface, and one question nobody can answer yet: where does everything go? A grandfather sits on a sealed box and says it's fine. Berakhot asks a bigger version of it. The Temple, God's house, is gone. Where does God live now?
screen: `HALF THE SIZE.` → `WHERE DOES EVERYTHING GO?` → `WHERE DOES GOD LIVE NOW?`

segments.voice: The answer, given in Ulla's name, is startlingly small: since the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One has nothing in the world but the four cubits of halakha. A cubit is an old measure, about the length of a forearm, and some readers picture four of them as the space around one person. Halakha is the Jewish way of living, the law walked out day by day. So the house of God shrinks, and lands in a space the size of a person doing the right thing. That changed how one sage lived. Abaye says: at first I used to study at home and pray in the synagogue. Once I heard this, I prayed only where I studied. The place where the learning happens became the holy place. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, after the Temple fell, God's whole place in the world became four cubits. That sounds like loss, and it is; the page doesn't pretend otherwise. But it's also portable. Four cubits fit in a dorm room, a kitchen corner, a chair by a hospital bed. Wherever someone sits down to learn and live it, there's room. A Temple-sized absence, and a person-sized answer.
screen: `THE TEMPLE IS GONE.` · `GOD'S PLACE: FOUR CUBITS OF HALAKHA.` · `ABAYE PRAYS WHERE HE STUDIES.` · `A PERSON-SIZED ANSWER.` · then, large: `FOUR CUBITS.`

segments.voice: Choose one small spot within reach: a corner of a desk, a shelf, a windowsill. Clear it if you can, and set one thing there that stands for what matters to you, a book, a candle, a photo. Sit facing it for the rest of the sit, and let that small space be enough.
Four cubits. After the Temple fell, the Talmud says, God's place in the world became the four cubits of halakha.
One to keep: four cubits, a person-sized room for something holy. That's Berakhot, day nine.

screen: `DAY 1496 COUNTS.` → `BERAKHOT · 9 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: A SWORD AT YOUR NECK. IS IT TOO LATE TO ASK?`

howItsDone: Many Jews keep a set place for prayer, a makom kavua, a custom discussed on these same pages of Berakhot, and some keep a small corner at home for study and prayer.

fork.setup: your cousin is starting college in a shared dorm room and worries there's no space to practice anything. what does Berakhot 8a offer?

wait until she finds a synagogue; a dorm can't be a holy place.
skip it for now; holiness needs its own room in a proper house.
fork.reveal: since the Temple fell, the Talmud says, God's place is four cubits of halakha. a dorm corner is the right size.

original.note: Hebrew: four cubits; with halakha, God's place in the world after the Temple fell.

options: Make one small corner for them. After the Temple, God's place was four cubits.
Wait for a bigger place; holy things need a proper room of their own.

chat.meaning: Berakhot 8a: since the Temple fell, God has only the four cubits of halakha. A small corner can hold something holy.

halakha.meaning: Jewish law: the way of living, walked out day by day

Ulla.meaning: a sage of the Talmud who traveled between Israel and Babylonia

Abaye.meaning: a leading sage of the Talmud in Babylonia

Temple.meaning: the holy Temple in Jerusalem, center of worship until it fell

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a (Rabbi Chiya bar Ami in Ulla's name: since the Temple was destroyed, God has only the four cubits of halakha; Abaye prays where he studies)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 6b (a fixed place for prayer, makom kavua)
